Mount Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan, standing 3,776 metres above sea level on the island of Honshu. It is an active stratovolcano that last erupted in 1707, and on a clear day it can be seen from Tokyo, about one hundred kilometres to the north-east. The mountain has an almost perfectly symmetrical cone, which is covered in snow for about five months of the year, and it has been a subject of Japanese art and poetry for centuries. Every summer, hundreds of thousands of people climb to the summit, most of them starting from one of the four fifth stations that can be reached by road. Many climbers set out in the evening and walk through the night, so that they can watch the sun rise from the top. The mountain was added to the World Heritage List in 2013 as a cultural site, because of the way it has inspired artists and pilgrims. Around its base there are five lakes, several hot springs, and a forest that grew on the lava of an eruption more than a thousand years ago. The railway company that runs the line to the northern foot of the mountain also operates buses to the trailheads during the climbing season, which lasts from early July to early September. Outside that season the huts are closed, the weather is severe, and the authorities ask people not to climb.

A bakery opens at six in the morning. The baker has been working since three, mixing the dough, shaping the loaves and lighting the ovens. By the time the first customers arrive, the shelves are full of bread, and the smell fills the whole street. Most people buy the same thing every day: a loaf of white bread, two rolls, or a pastry to eat on the way to work. On Saturdays the queue reaches the corner, because that is the day the baker makes the dark rye bread that his grandfather taught him to bake.
